strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: targeted concept unlearning for text-to-video diffusion models, where prior training-free editing methods (UCE, RECE) were designed for image models only.

The proposed method is simple, training-free, and fully closed-form: refusal vectors from a handful (5) of paired safe/unsafe prompts, refined via contrastive PCA into a low-rank subspace, and absorbed into FFN weights with no added parameters or inference latency. The weight-update derivation in the appendix is carefully worked out (norm preservation, scalar commutation).

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation protocol using the T2VSafetyBench benchmark across five unsafe categories, with both quantitative (censorship rate, MM-Notox, FVD) and extensive qualitative results across all categories in the appendix.

Useful ablation studies on the cPCA rank (finding an intermediate rank ~100 is optimal) and the suppression coefficient λ (showing a monotonic censorship/quality trade-off), plus a layer-wise sweep justifying editing only the final three double blocks.
Honest limitations section discussing misuse potential, adversarial reversibility of the injected direction, and single-concept removal.
weaknesses: No baselines whatsoever. The paper claims to be the first video unlearning method, but it does not compare against any reasonable alternative: adapted UCE/RECE, fine-tuning (Forget-Me-Not style), inference-time filtering/steering (Safe Latent Diffusion, SteerDiff), or simple prompt-level defenses. Without such comparisons, it is impossible to judge whether the proposed approach is actually superior or merely convenient.

The central claim of 'inherently more robust against adversarial bypass attempts compared to surface-level input-output filters' appears in the abstract and related work but is never experimentally evaluated — no adversarial attack experiments are reported at all.

A likely technical inconsistency: the low-rank subspace is derived from the covariance of N=5 centered pair differences, whose rank is at most 4, yet the ablation reports an optimal cPCA rank of k=100 (and tests up to thousands). This suggests either more data is used than stated, or the derivation/protocol is not accurately described. This should be clarified.

The FVD analysis is non-standard: FVD is reported only between unsafe and neutralized video sets (196) rather than against a real-video reference distribution, and comparison to 'pure noise' (947) is not a meaningful quality reference. There is no standard fidelity metric (e.g., FVD against real videos, CLIP text-video alignment) on benign prompts to quantify retention of general generation quality.

Evaluation is restricted to a single model (Open-Sora), a modified T2VSafetyBench protocol (recomputed baselines, subset of categories), and relies entirely on a GPT-4 frame-level judge without any human verification in this paper. Residual censorship rates remain substantial for some categories (e.g., 33% for Copyright/Trademarks).

The claimed contribution of using both text and image conditioning for concept extraction is asserted as a key contribution with '(as supported by experiments)', but no such ablation (multimodal vs. text-only) is actually shown in the paper.

Quantitative retention/forgetting is mostly qualitative; there is no quantitative measure of collateral forgetting on unrelated concepts, despite this being a primary motivation of the low-rank/cPCA design.
Presentation issues: empty 'Project page:' link, several typos, and figures with small/unlabeled axis details in the ablation plots.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: concept unlearning for video diffusion models, which prior training-free weight-editing methods (UCE, RECE) do not cover.
The proposed pipeline is simple and practical: a closed-form weight edit requiring only 5 safe/unsafe prompt pairs, no retraining, and no inference-time overhead.

The paper includes some ablation studies (cPCA rank, suppression coefficient lambda) and a layer-selection analysis in the appendix, and reports results on the T2VSafetyBench protocol across five concept categories.
The mathematical derivation of the weight update (appendix B) is provided in detail and appears correct, supporting reproducibility of the core edit operation.
weaknesses: No baselines whatsoever. The evaluation compares only against the unmodified OPEN-SORA model. There is no comparison against any unlearning approach (e.g., fine-tuning-based erasure, ESD/UCE/RECE adapted to video, Safe Latent Diffusion, or even a simple prompt-negative/inference-filter baseline), so it is impossible to judge whether the method is competitive or how much of the gain comes from the low-rank/cPCA machinery versus any generic suppression.

Several key claims are unsupported by experiments. The introduction advertises an ablation showing 'only 0.8% of the original space is needed' and a key contribution on using both text and image conditioning to 'prevent forgetting', but the ablation section (4.4) only covers cPCA rank and lambda; neither the modality ablation nor the subspace-dimension claim appears in the paper. Similarly, the claim of improved 'robustness against adversarial bypass attempts' is never tested with any attack.

Effectiveness is far from complete and inconsistently reported: after unlearning, 33% of Copyright/Trademark and 13.4% of Pornography generations still contain unsafe content, with no analysis of failure modes. There is no human evaluation; all safety assessment relies on a GPT-4 frame-level binary classifier whose reliability in this new setting is assumed from prior work on a different benchmark setup.

The quality/forgetting evaluation is weak. MM-Notox differences of ~2-5% are small and no significance testing or variance over seeds is reported. FVD is computed between unsafe and censored sets of the same model rather than against real data, making absolute values (144-284) hard to interpret; there is no retain-set forgetting metric quantifying collateral damage on unrelated concepts, despite that being a central claimed advantage.

Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a combination of known ingredients — difference-in-means 'refusal directions' (Arditi et al.), contrastive PCA (Abid et al.), and low-rank weight projection edits — applied to a new architecture. The application is new, but the methodological contribution is incremental and the paper does not analyze why or when the linear-direction assumption holds for video diffusion.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: typos and grammatical errors throughout ('The images has been manually censored', 'healty', 'relatively the left- and right-singular vectors'), an empty 'Project page' link, inconsistent numbers (abstract/contribution claims 5 prompt pairs while the public-figures appendix lists 5 names but earlier text and figures imply different counts), and illegibly small ablation plots (Figure 3).

Important methodological details that strongly affect results (which layers to edit, hyperparameters alpha, k, lambda per category) are tuned post hoc (e.g., layers 17-19 selected via sweep), with no discussion of sensitivity or generalization to other architectures, raising overfitting-to-benchmark concerns.
The limitations section itself concedes adversarial reversibility of the vector and single-concept-at-a-time removal, which directly contradicts the abstract's safety-robustness framing.

strengths: Addresses an important and relatively unexplored problem: concept unlearning for text-to-video diffusion models, where prior work (UCE, RECE) targets image models only

Simple, training-free method with a closed-form weight update; the appendix provides a careful derivation showing the subspace-aware correction can be absorbed into the FFN weights with no inference-time overhead
Evaluation on a recognized safety benchmark (T2VSafetyBench) across five unsafe categories, with both quantitative (censorship rate, MM-Notox, FVD) and extensive qualitative results
Ablation studies on the cPCA rank and the suppression coefficient λ, showing sensible behavior and a tunable trade-off between censorship strength and visual fidelity
Honest limitations section acknowledging misuse risks, adversarial reversibility, and single-concept scope
weaknesses: No baseline comparisons. The paper only compares the original model vs. its edited version. There are no comparisons against obvious alternatives such as adapting UCE/RECE to the video setting, inference-time steering, Safe Latent Diffusion-style filtering, negative prompting, or simple prompt filtering. Claims of superiority over 'surface-level input-output filters' are asserted but never tested, and the adversarial-robustness claim in the abstract is entirely unsupported by experiments

A claimed key contribution—the use of both text and image conditioning for concept extraction 'as supported by experiments'—has no corresponding ablation table or figure in the paper. The ablation section covers only cPCA rank and λ, so this central claim is not actually evidenced

Limited methodological novelty: the approach is largely a combination of existing techniques (activation-difference refusal vectors from Arditi et al., contrastive PCA from Abid et al., subspace projection), adapted to video. The main novelty is the application domain

Narrow evaluation scope: only one backbone (Open-Sora), five concept categories, and a very small number of curated prompt pairs (N=5). No statistical significance, confidence intervals, or discussion of sample sizes for the GPT-4-based censorship rates (e.g., 10%→2% for Public Figures appears to be over very few videos)

Collateral-damage / generalization claims are weakly supported: preservation of quality on benign, unrelated prompts is asserted but not quantitatively evaluated on a held-out set of safe prompts; the FVD of ~196 between unsafe and neutralized videos is a strange, weakly interpretable metric

Inconsistencies and clarity issues: the abstract says '5 multi-modal prompt pairs' while Figure 1 says 'image-prompt pairs'; how image-conditioning pairs are constructed is never explained (Appendix D lists only text prompts); notation inconsistencies between Eq. (3), (6), (13) (r̂ vs r*); typos ('Substituing', 'healty', 'The images has been'); the project page is empty in the submitted version
Evaluation relies solely on an automated GPT-4 judge; no human evaluation is provided to validate the censorship and quality judgments

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: permanent (weight-level) unlearning for text-to-video diffusion models, where prior work is either inference-time filtering (SAFREE, VideoEraser) or costly fine-tuning (NullSCE). The claim of the first training-free closed-form weight update for video diffusion is well-motivated and, as far as I can verify, not contradicted by cited literature.

Comprehensive evaluation: two models (Open-Sora, ZeroScopeT2V), two established benchmarks (T2VSafetyBench, SafeSora), and three complementary metrics (censorship rate, FVD, MM-Notox), with comparisons to both a filtering baseline and a fine-tuning baseline, plus an adapted UCE evaluation in Appendix F.

Thorough ablation study: rank k of the cPCA subspace, suppression strength λ, layer selection, sensitivity to safe/unsafe pair choice, robustness to neutral-set resampling, and refusal-only vs. PCA vs. cPCA comparisons.

Useful supplementary analyses: multi-concept (multi-vector) unlearning experiments, FVMD temporal-coherence results, computational cost comparison (~$1, 10 forward passes vs. thousands of GPU-hours), and an adversarial-prompting robustness test showing only 4% unsafe frames after attack.

Clear derivation (Appendix B) showing the inference-time projection is exactly absorbable into the subsequent linear layer weights, with no inference overhead — the central technical claim is soundly supported.
Full prompt sets for refusal vector construction and code/videos promised for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the core ingredients (mean difference-in-activations refusal direction from LLM interpretability, PCA truncation, contrastive PCA, rank-one weight editing à la UCE) are all established techniques; the contribution is primarily their adaptation and combination for the video diffusion setting rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Single-concept operation: the method requires a separately constructed set of five handcrafted safe/unsafe prompt pairs per concept, and the multi-vector experiment (Table 8) shows quality degradation (sharp FVD rise, e.g., 579 on action-risk prompts) when composing five concepts. Scalability to many concepts and how these prompts are authored/certified is underexplored.

Evaluation concerns: (i) NullSCE results for the Gore category are missing in Table 1, weakening the fine-tuning comparison; (ii) in Table 6 the 'censored' FVMD is consistently lower (better) than the baseline across most categories, which is surprising for a censoring intervention and deserves explanation; (iii) safety judging relies on a single GPT-4o evaluator with per-frame YES/NO aggregation, and some ablations are run only on small subsets (e.g., 100 prompts), limiting statistical strength; (iv) FVD is computed against limited reference sets, where small differences are hard to interpret.

Key hyperparameters (layers 17–18, λ=1, k=100, α=1) are hand-selected empirically; the layer-selection discussion is brief and the optimal-rank behavior in Figure 3 (sharp non-monotonicity) suggests possible sensitivity on other models/categories.

Some inconsistencies in the narrative: censorship reductions are variously reported as averages of 36.3%/58.2% (abstract), 'up to 72%', and 'up to 69.6%', which makes precise claim verification difficult; minor typos and rough writing throughout (e.g., 'relatively' for 'respectively', 'healty', citation formatting errors like 'Ziegler et al., 1909').

The permanent/irreversible weight edit property is presented as a benefit but its security implications (e.g., against concept resurgence, as noted for other unlearning methods by Suriyakumar et al. 2024) are not deeply analyzed; the adversarial test is limited to one attack on one category.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: existing video-diffusion safety methods are either inference-time filters (SAFREE, VideoEraser) that can be bypassed, or weight-level approaches requiring costly fine-tuning (NullSCE); a training-free, closed-form weight update for T2V models is a useful and previously unclaimed contribution.
The weight-absorption derivation (Appendix B) is carefully worked out, with correct handling of the orthonormal-projection norm preservation and closed-form rank-k update of the linear layers.

Reasonably broad evaluation: two models (Open-Sora, ZeroScopeT2V), two benchmarks (T2VSafetyBench, SafeSora), multiple metrics (censorship rate, FVD, FVMD, MM-Notox), plus additional ablations on cPCA rank, suppression strength, prompt-pair similarity, neutral-set stability, cPCA vs. PCA, multi-vector composition, and an adapted UCE baseline.
Efficiency claims are concrete and credible (0.4 GPU-hours, ~$1, only 5 prompt pairs per concept), and the adversarial-prompt robustness check is a welcome addition.
Strong censorship-rate reductions (e.g., 68.1% to 9.9% on SafeSora) while FVD remains broadly comparable to the baseline.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is an assembly of established components — refusal/activation directions from LLM interpretability (Arditi et al., 2024), projection-based concept removal from image diffusion, and contrastive PCA (Abid et al., 2018) — adapted to video. The technical contribution is a straightforward transposition, and the paper's repeated 'first' claims rely on fairly narrow definitions.

Comparisons are confounded by model choice: NullSCE is only compared on Open-Sora/T2VSafetyBench and SAFREE only on ZeroScopeT2V/SafeSora. There is no setting where both baselines and the proposed method are evaluated on the same model and benchmark, weakening the claim of superiority over the state of the art.

Heavy reliance on a GPT-4o frame-level judge for the primary metric (censorship rate), with no human evaluation reported; judge-based safety metrics are known to be noisy and gameable, and the frame-level YES/NO aggregation procedure is under-specified.

Metric presentation is inconsistent and sometimes contradicts the claims: MM-Notox is defined such that lower is better and claimed to show 'improved alignment', yet several categories increase after unlearning (e.g., Sexual 22.26→22.62, Animal Abuse 22.73→22.85); FVD degrades noticeably on Public Figures (160.98→176.50) and on some SafeSora categories, which is downplayed in the text.

The claim of 'permanent/irreversible' unlearning is asserted but never tested against concept resurgence or relearning, despite the authors themselves citing Suriyakumar et al. (2024) showing exactly this failure mode in diffusion unlearning.

Robustness of results is under-supported: no error bars, seeds, or variance estimates on the main tables; sensitive hyperparameters (layers 17–18, λ=1, k=100) are chosen empirically and the ablations are limited to single categories/subsets.

Clarity and polish issues undermine confidence: 'Project page:' is empty, citation errors (e.g., 'Ziegler et al., 1909'), repeated misuse of 'relatively' for 'respectively', several incomplete cells and dashes in Table 8, and Figure 3's axis labels are illegible.

Qualitative results are only mildly persuasive: some 'censored' outputs show subtle changes (added railing, softened gore), and the per-category censorship rates remain non-trivial (e.g., 22.2% on Animal Abuse), leaving a meaningful residual risk that the safety framing overstates.

strengths: Addresses a clear and important gap: prior video diffusion safety methods either filter at inference (SAFREE, VideoEraser) without permanence, or require costly fine-tuning (NullSCE). The proposed training-free, closed-form weight update fills a genuine niche in the video unlearning landscape.

Technically coherent method: refusal direction estimation from safe/unsafe activation pairs, subspace projection via truncated SVD, contrastive PCA (cPCA) to reduce collateral forgetting, and a clean derivation (Appendix B) showing the activation-level edit can be exactly absorbed into the linear layer weights with no inference overhead.

Comprehensive evaluation across two models (Open-Sora, ZeroScopeT2V) and two benchmarks (T2VSafetyBench, SafeSora) with three complementary metrics (censorship rate, FVD, MM-Notox), plus extended metrics (FVMD) and cost-efficiency comparison (Table 7).

Strong ablation and robustness coverage: cPCA rank, lambda, layer selection, prompt-pair sensitivity, neutral-set stability, refusal vs. PCA vs. cPCA, UCE adaptation with a full hyperparameter study (Appendix F), multi-vector mass erasure (Appendix C.3), and adversarial prompt attacks (Appendix H, only 4% unsafe-frame resurgence).
Reproducibility support: code provided, full prompt sets for refusal vectors disclosed (Appendix E), implementation details per backbone architecture.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially a composition of existing techniques — refusal/ablation directions from LLM interpretability (Arditi et al., 2024), projection-based concept removal akin to UCE/RECE, and contrastive PCA (Abid et al., 2018). The contribution is primarily adaptation to video diffusion rather than a new principle.

Incomplete head-to-head baseline comparisons: NullSCE is only compared on Open-Sora/T2VSafetyBench and SAFREE only on ZeroScopeT2V/SafeSora. There is no table where all methods are evaluated on the same model–benchmark combination, making the claim of 'outperforming the state-of-the-art' weaker than it appears, since effects of model and method are confounded.

Residual unsafe rates remain non-trivial (12.6% and 9.9% on average), and Public Figures censorship is only 2–7% at baseline, limiting the practical significance of gains in some categories. The safety-improvement framing slightly overstates what is achieved.

Metric concerns: censorship is judged by a GPT-4o evaluator whose reliability on video frames is asserted by citation rather than verified in this work; FVD is computed against unspecified real reference sets with unclear sample sizes; FVD scale differs dramatically between Table 1 (~150-180) and Table 2 (~55-95) without explanation; Public Figures FVD degrades (160.98 to 176.50) while being described as stable.

Hyperparameters (layers 17–18, k=100, five prompt pairs) are tuned empirically per model, and it is unclear how sensitive or transferable these choices are to newer video backbones (e.g., HunyuanVideo, CogVideoX); only two relatively older models are tested.

Some inconsistencies in the multi-concept results (Table 8): e.g., Copyright censorship stays at ~41-42% with 2-3 vectors and only drops with 5 vectors at a sharp FVD cost, and several cells are missing, undermining the mass-erasure claim.

Manuscript quality issues: empty project page link, duplicated reference entries (Wang et al. 2023a/b; Ziegler with erroneous '1909'), grammatical errors, and Figure 4's low-resolution presentation reduce polish.
